notes.17:8: The Greek preserves the distinct Levite names Samuas, Manthanias, Jasiel, and Tobadobiah (where the Hebrew reads Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Asahel, and two separate names, Tobijah and Tobadonijah).
notes.17:11: The Greek mentions only the seven thousand seven hundred rams and omits the seven thousand seven hundred male goats found in the Hebrew text.
notes.17:16: The Greek reads the distinct name "Masaiah the son of Zari" where the Hebrew reads "Amasiah the son of Zichri."
notes.18:7: The Greek reads the distinct name "Jemaa" (Greek Iemaas here and Iemaa in 18:8) where the Hebrew reads "Imlah."
notes.18:10: The Greek reads the distinct name "Canaan" (here and in 18:23) where the Hebrew reads "Chenaanah."
notes.18:23: The repetitive phrasing in Zedekiah's question ("a spirit from me—a spirit to you, the Spirit of the Lord from me") reflects a textual doublet in the Septuagint tradition, where the finite verb of motion is ellipsed.
notes.18:25: The Greek reads the distinct name "Emer" where the Hebrew reads "Amon," and adds the title "the ruler" for Joash.
notes.18:29: The Greek reads "Disguise me ... put on my apparel," whereas the Hebrew reads "I will disguise myself ... put on your robes."
notes.18:33: The Greek reads "with sure aim" and "between the lung and the breastplate," whereas the Hebrew reads "at random" and "between the joints of the armor."
notes.19:2: The Greek includes the direct address "O King Jehoshaphat" and uses the passive "one who is hated by the Lord" where the Hebrew reads "those who hate the LORD."
notes.19:8: The Greek reads "to judge those who dwell in Jerusalem," whereas the Hebrew reads "for controversies; and they returned to Jerusalem."
notes.19:10: The Greek syntax here is compressed, reading "our brethren" (first person) and omitting "in their cities" as well as the second mention of bloodshed found in the Hebrew text.
notes.20:14: The Greek text gives the lineage as Oziel son of Zechariah, of the sons of Eleael son of Manthanias, differing from the Hebrew text (Jahaziel son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah).
notes.20:16: "Hasae" and "Jeriel" follow the Greek proper names (corresponding to Ziz and Jeruel in the Hebrew text); similarly, 20:2 reads "Hasam Thamara" (for Hazazon Tamar) and 20:17 reads "Behold also Jerusalem."
notes.20:22: Where the Hebrew text mentions "ambushes," the Greek states that the Lord caused the sons of Ammon to wage war against Moab and Mount Seir.
notes.20:34: The Greek text reads "Joshua" (Iesou) rather than "Jehu," and has the singular "who wrote the book of the king of Israel."
notes.20:37: "Eleiada the son of Odeia" preserves the Greek proper names, corresponding to Eliezer the son of Dodavahu in the Hebrew text.
notes.21:2: Although the Greek text states that Jehoram had six brothers, it lists only four names (Jehiel, Zechariah, Mishael, and Shephatiah), omitting the two occurrences of Azariah found in the Hebrew text.
notes.21:9: The Greek text reads "all the cavalry" (rather than "all the chariots") and includes the closing clause "and the people fled to their tents," paralleling 2 Kings 8:21.
notes.21:17: The Greek text reads "his daughters" (where the Hebrew has "his wives") and names the surviving son "Ahaziah" (rather than "Jehoahaz").
notes.21:19: The Greek renders the Hebrew idiom for "two years" literally as "two days," and refers to a "funeral" (ekphora) rather than a ritual burning.
notes.22:1: "The Alimazoneans" preserves a unique Greek proper name (Aleimazoneis) where the Hebrew text refers to those who came with the Arabians to the camp.
notes.22:2: The Greek text gives Ahaziah's accession age as twenty years (closer to 2 Kings 8:26), rather than forty-two years as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.22:6: The Greek text reads "Israel" twice here instead of "Jezreel."
notes.22:7: The Greek text is elliptical here, omitting Jehu's name before "the son of Nimshi" and lacking an explicit verb before "the house of Ahab."
notes.23:1: The Greek text reads "eighth year" (Hebrew MT: "seventh year") and "with him into the house" (MT: "into a covenant with him"), and preserves the LXX-distinct names Azeiah (MT: Adaiah) and Elishaphan son of Zechariah (MT: Elishaphat son of Zichri).
notes.23:13: "Conspiring, you conspire!" literally renders the Greek participle-and-verb construction corresponding to the Hebrew exclamation "Treason! Treason!"
notes.23:20: The Septuagint reads "brought the king up into the house of the Lord" and "the inner gate," whereas the Hebrew MT reads "brought the king down from the house of the Lord" and "the Upper Gate."
notes.24:1: The Septuagint preserves the LXX-distinct name Abia for the mother of Joash (Hebrew MT: Zibiah).
notes.24:5: The Greek reads "make haste to speak" and "Yet the Levites did not believe," differing from the Hebrew MT ("hasten the matter; but the Levites did not hasten").
notes.24:13: "The length of the works went up in their hands" renders the literal Greek wording, where the translator read the Hebrew term for "restoration" or "healing" as "length."
notes.24:20: The Septuagint identifies the priest as Azariah the son of Jehoiada, whereas the Hebrew MT calls him Zechariah.
notes.24:26: The Septuagint preserves the distinct names Zabel son of Sama and Zozabed son of Somaioth (Hebrew MT: Zabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shimrith), and continues directly into verse 27 ("and all his sons, and the five came to him"), where the Greek diverges markedly from the Hebrew MT.
notes.25:1: The Greek text gives Amaziah's mother's name as Jonaa (Ionaa), corresponding to Jehoaddan in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.25:8: The Greek reads "if you suppose to prevail by these, then the Lord will put you to flight," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's ironic command to go and be strong in battle.
notes.25:17: The Greek text preserves only this brief clause, omitting Amaziah's message challenging Joash king of Israel found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.25:18: "Thistle" translates two Greek transliterations (chozei and achouch) of the Hebrew word for thornbush or thistle; the Greek also includes a future-tense clause before the wild beasts trample it.
notes.25:25: The Greek identifies the king of Israel as "Joash the son of Joash," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Joash the son of Jehoahaz."
notes.26:1: The Greek text names the new king Ahaziah (Ochozeias) in this verse, whereas from verse 3 onward it calls him Uzziah (Ozeias).
notes.26:3: The Greek gives Uzziah's mother's name as Chaia (Chaaia), corresponding to Jecoliah in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.26:6: The Greek reads Abner (Abenner) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the Philistine city of Jabneh.
notes.26:21: "A separate house" renders the Greek en oiko aphphousion, which transliterates the Hebrew term for a house of isolation or seclusion.
notes.26:22: The Greek attributes this record to "Jesse the prophet" (Iesseiou), reflecting an early variant for "Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:1: The Greek gives the name of Jerusha's father as Sador, corresponding to Zadok in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:4: The Greek text continues the verb "he built" from verse 3 without repeating it and omits the mention of "cities" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:5: The Greek includes "in the first year" along with the second and third years of Ammon's tribute, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text lists only the second and third years.
notes.27:9: Verse 8, which repeats Jotham's age at accession and length of reign in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, is absent from this Greek text.
notes.28:3: "Gaibenthom" is the Septuagint's transliteration of the Valley of Ben-Hinnom; the Greek also reads "and the abominations" (rendered "along with the abominations") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "according to the abominations."
notes.28:6: The Greek text reads "sent" (apesteilen), a distinctive Septuagint reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Greek witnesses read "slew" (apekteinen).
notes.28:8: The Septuagint specifies "three hundred thousand" captives, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "two hundred thousand."
notes.28:10: The Greek reads "to bear witness to the Lord our God," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's reference to "guilt" against God.
notes.28:18: The Septuagint lists "Galero" and "Galezo" (omitting Timnah) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has Gederoth and Gimzo; similarly, distinctive Greek personal names appear in 28:7 ("Egdreikan") and 28:12 ("Oudeia," "Zechariah," and "Choad").
notes.29:1: The Septuagint names Hezekiah's mother "Abba," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Abijah."
notes.29:12: Several Levitical names in 29:12–14 preserve distinctive Septuagint forms—including "Masi," "Zechariah," "Elle," "Zemmath," "Jodan," "Zambri," "Asa," and "Azariah"—and the Greek groups those of Zemmath and Jodan together as sons of Joah.
notes.29:17: The Septuagint dates the start of the purification to "the third day, the new moon of the first month" and its completion to "the thirteenth day," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads the first day and the sixteenth day.
notes.29:33: The Septuagint records "three thousand five hundred sheep," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "three thousand."
notes.30:6: The Greek reads an imperative ("bring back those who have escaped") with singular "the king of Assyria" and "the God of Abraham" (without "the Lord"), whereas the Hebrew reads "that He may return to the remnant ... from the hand of the kings of Assyria."
notes.30:11: The Greek places "and into Judah" at the end of verse 11 rather than at the start of verse 12, and uses the verb "turned" (denoting repentance) where the Hebrew has "humbled themselves."
notes.30:24: The Greek reads "to Judah, to the assembly" and ends with "and the consecrated offerings of the priests were in great abundance," differing from the Hebrew ("Hezekiah king of Judah" and "a great number of priests consecrated themselves").
notes.31:6: Following the Greek verse division that places "the children of Israel and Judah" at the end of verse 5, verse 6 reads "tithes of goats" where the Hebrew reads "tithes of the holy things."
notes.31:13: The Greek preserves several distinct personal names here (Uzziah, Maeth, Ezabath, Jeiel, Thanai) and adds "and his sons" after Benaiah; verse 12 also spells Conaniah as Chomenias in the Greek text.
notes.31:14: The Greek names Kore's father as Heman (Hebrew: Imnah), and verse 15 preserves the Greek-distinct names Odom, Benjamin, Shimei, and Marias alongside "through the hand of the priests" (Hebrew: "in the cities of the priests").
notes.31:21: The Greek reads "with all his soul" where the Hebrew reads "with all his heart."
notes.32:18: The Greek reads "to help them and to pull down" (boethesai autois kai kataspasai), likely an early inner-Greek scribal shift from phobesai ("to frighten"), corresponding to "to frighten them and terrify them" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.32:28: The Greek reads "cities" (poleis) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "storehouses."
notes.32:30: The Greek reads "Zion" (Seion) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Gihon."
notes.32:31: The Greek reads "the Lord" (Kyrios) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "God."
notes.33:6: "Ge-Bane-Hinnom" preserves the Septuagint transliteration (ge bane Hennom) of the Hebrew phrase meaning "the valley of the sons of Hinnom."
notes.33:14: The Greek reads "at the exit of the gate round about, and even to Ophel [Greek Opla] itself," omitting "Fish" before "Gate" as found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.33:17: The Greek is elliptical, omitting the verb "sacrificed" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and placing "the Lord their God" in the nominative case.
notes.33:19: The Greek reads "in the words of the seers" (ton horonton) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the chronicles of Hozai."
notes.33:20: Here and throughout verses 21-25, the Greek names Manasseh's son "Amos" (Amos) rather than "Amon" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.34:8: The Greek text gives the names "Selia" (for Hebrew Azaliah), "Maasa" (for Maaseiah), and "Joach" (for Joahaz).
notes.34:12: The Greek text reads "Ie" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "Jahath."
notes.34:20: The Greek text reads "Abdodom" (for Hebrew Abdon) and "Isaiah" (for Hebrew Asaiah).
notes.34:22: The Greek reads "Kathual" and "Chelles" (for Hebrew Tokhath and Hasrah), applies a feminine participle to Huldah as "who kept the commandments" (where the Hebrew calls Shallum "keeper of the wardrobe"), and transliterates the Jerusalem quarter as "Maasanai" (Hebrew Mishneh, the Second Quarter).
notes.35:3: The Greek describes the Levites as "capable in all Israel" (Hebrew "who taught all Israel") and narrates the placing of the ark as an accomplished act ("they placed") rather than a command.
notes.35:9: The Greek includes "Benaiah" in the list of Levite leaders and reads "Joel" where the Hebrew has "Jeiel."
notes.35:12: The Greek reads "for the morning" (reflecting unpointed Hebrew labboqer rather than labbaqar, "for the cattle"); similarly in 35:13, "and it prospered" reflects the verb tzalach ("prosper") rather than "in pans."
notes.35:19: The Greek preserves an extended section paralleling 2 Kings 23:24-27 not found in the Hebrew of 2 Chronicles, including the untranslated term "karasim" (for abominations) and "ordinances" where 2 Kings 23:26 has "provocations."
notes.35:25: The Greek reads "all the rulers and the female rulers," reflecting Hebrew sarim/sarot ("rulers") rather than sharim/sharot ("singers").
notes.36:2: The Greek text includes material parallel to 2 Kings 23:31–33 and preserves the distinct proper names Abital (Hebrew Hamutal) and Dablatha (Hebrew Riblah).
notes.36:5: The Greek text expands Jehoiakim's reign with material parallel to 2 Kings 23:36–24:4, naming his mother Zechora, daughter of Neriah from Ramah, attributing the innocent blood to Jehoiakim, and concluding that the Lord was not willing to destroy them (contrast Hebrew "to pardon").
notes.36:8: "Ganozae" is a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew phrase gan-Uzza ("the garden of Uzza"; cf. 2 Kings 21:18, 26), and the Greek names Jehoiakim's successor Jeconiah (Hebrew Jehoiachin).
notes.36:17: The Greek text reads "he did not spare Zedekiah" (where the Hebrew has "young man") and shifts to plural verbs for the Chaldeans before returning to the Lord as subject of "He delivered."
notes.36:23: The Greek places "to all the kingdoms of the earth" in the dative as the addressees of Cyrus's decree, leaving the object of "has given" implicit (supplied as "them"); likewise in 36:20 the Greek reads "of the Medes" where the Hebrew reads "of Persia."
